Each cost component was distributed across all hours of the year based on the system's total load (net or gross) during each hour, as shown in Figure 1. This configuration represents the most dynamic tariff design, providing the strongest price signals to customers regarding optimal load adjustments. However, alternative tariff designs are feasible, where only a subset of cost components is allocated dynamically. In this study, we employ three dynamic price design scenarios, with cost component allocation on an hourly basis. Any costs not allocated dynamically are charged on a fixed volumetric basis, implying that the hourly price for that component remains constant throughout the year. The price design scenarios are as follows: ● Full: 100% of revenues allocated dynamically, 0% flat, as in previous studies ● Medium: 50% of revenues allocated dynamically, 50% flat ● Mild: 20% of revenues allocated dynamically, 80% flat. 8 Figure 1. Hourly 2019 universal tariff breakdown for the Full dynamic tariff by cost components for PGE (top), SCE (middle), and SDGE (bottom) during peak net load week in 2019 2.2.2 Price forecasting To develop future price profiles, an understanding of trends in electric revenue requirements and rates is crucial. In this analysis, we considered two scenarios using the information from two different sources and identified the associated average annual increase in rates for each IOU in each source. We then apply these growth rates to project average electricity costs from 2026 to 2030. The source information includes: ● Revenue requests approved by CPUC through general rate case (GRC) for 2019 and submitted itemized lists of revenue requests for IOUs up to 2026. ○ 14.72% annual growth for PGE, 10.78% for SCE, and 7.78% for SDGE ● Nominal historical and projected inflation-adjusted bundled residential customer rates from the Senate Bill 695 report between 2016 to 2019 and 2023 to 2026 (excluding 2020 to 2022 due to the anticipated impacts of the 2019 wildfire events and recovery efforts) ○ 5.04% annual growth for PGE, 3.94% for SCE, and 8.12% for SDGE Therefore, the 2030 High price scenario considers the higher of the two growth rates from each dataset, while the 2030 Low considers the lower. This means that the high scenario consists of the growth rates from item 1 (i.e., the entire 2019-2026 period) for PG&E and SCE, and the rates from item 2 (with 2020-2022 omitted) for SDG&E, and vice versa for the low scenario.
